subject: anatomy
title: Brainstem anatomy: midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata

steps.tx: The **brainstem** connects the cerebral hemispheres with the spinal cord, comprising the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata. It houses ascending sensory tracts, descending motor tracts and nuclei of cranial nerves three through twelve. It integrates vital autonomic centers controlling respiration, cardiovascular tone and consciousness through the reticular activating system. The fourth ventricle lies posterior to the pons and upper medulla.

steps.tx: The **pyramidal decussation** marks the junction between the closed medulla oblongata and the cervical spinal cord. Approximately eighty-five percent of descending corticospinal fibres cross the anterior median fissure to form the lateral corticospinal tract. The remaining uncrossed fibres continue as the anterior corticospinal tract. This anatomical crossover explains why a unilateral cerebral motor cortex lesion produces contralateral hemiparesis below the neck.

steps.tx: Brainstem vascular syndromes produce pathognomonic alternating neurological deficits. **Wallenberg syndrome** or lateral medullary syndrome results from occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery or vertebral artery. It damages the nucleus ambiguus, producing dysphagia and hoarseness; the spinal trigeminal nucleus, causing ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss; the spinothalamic tract, causing contralateral body sensory loss; and sympathetic descending fibres, causing Horner syndrome.

steps.tx: The **midbrain** surrounds the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius. Dorsally, the superior colliculi coordinate visual reflexes, while the inferior colliculi relay auditory signals to the medial geniculate body. Ventrally, the substantia nigra contains dopaminergic neurons projecting to the striatum, which degenerate in Parkinson disease. The red nucleus gives origin to the rubrospinal tract, coordinating flexor tone.
